questions.q: Name the two basic body forms exhibited by cnidarians and give one example of each.
questions.a: The two body forms are polyp (sessile, cylindrical; example: Hydra) and medusa (free-swimming, umbrella-shaped; example: Aurelia). A wrong answer (e.g., naming "larva" and "adult" or confusing polyp with medusa) reveals the student has not grasped the fundamental morphological distinction that defines cnidarian polymorphism and life cycles.

questions.q: Why is the gastrovascular cavity of cnidarians considered "incomplete" despite performing both digestion and circulation?
questions.a: It is incomplete because it has only a single opening serving as both mouth and anus, so ingestion and egestion occur through the same aperture — unlike a complete digestive system with separate mouth and anus. A student who says "it's incomplete because it lacks enzymes" confuses structural completeness with digestive mode; extracellular digestion occurs in both complete and incomplete systems.

questions.q: A student observes a colonial cnidarian where some individuals are feeding polyps (gastrozooids) and others are reproductive medusae (gonozooids). Which class does it likely belong to, and what phenomenon does this illustrate?
questions.a: It belongs to Hydrozoa and illustrates polymorphism (division of labour among zooids). A wrong answer like "Scyphozoa" or "metagenesis" shows confusion: Scyphozoa are predominantly medusoid with reduced polyp stage, and metagenesis refers to alternation of generations, not simultaneous functional specialisation within a colony.

questions.q: Compare the mesoglea in Hydrozoa, Scyphozoa, and Anthozoa. How does its composition relate to the dominant body form?
questions.a: Hydrozoa: thin, acellular mesoglea (polyp-dominant); Scyphozoa: thick, cellular mesoglea with amoebocytes (medusa-dominant, provides buoyancy); Anthozoa: cellular mesoglea with fibrous connective tissue (polyp-only, supports heavy skeleton). A student who describes all mesoglea as "acellular jelly" fails to link mesoglea cellularity to mechanical demands of the dominant life form — a key evolutionary adaptation.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Metagenesis in Obelia is identical to alternation of generations in plants because both involve haploid and diploid stages."
questions.a: The claim is false. In Obelia, both polyp (asexual) and medusa (sexual) are diploid; meiosis occurs only during gamete formation in medusae (gametic meiosis). In plants, alternation of generations involves multicellular haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) stages with sporic meiosis. A student who agrees conflates life cycle patterns — a critical error in understanding animal vs. plant reproductive strategies.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a live Hydra specimen to demonstrate that nematocyst discharge is triggered by both mechanical and chemical stimuli.
questions.a: Place Hydra in a watch glass with pond water. (1) Touch a tentacle with a fine glass needle — observe immediate coiling and nematocyst discharge (mechanical trigger). (2) Add a drop of glutathione (reduced) solution — observe massive nematocyst discharge without contact (chemical trigger). (3) Control: add distilled water — no discharge. A poor design (e.g., only testing touch) misses the dual-trigger mechanism essential for prey capture in nature.
